projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edmund B. Storms was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Edmund B. Storms. Mr. Storms served in the U.S. Army and the European Theater. And his highest rank was T5. I am Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Storms' home in Stow, Ohio on February 20, 2004. Ed was 81 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: In 1941, I was living at Michigan State. We were going to college. And it was on November -- let's see, what was it, December 7 that we -- that the battle in Japan started. And I remember it well because Bob was -- we were roommates together at Wells Hall at Michigan State in East Lansing, Michigan. And he was doing his first oil painting. And, of course, he and I worked very close together on his artwork. And I just remember it was a couple of hunting dogs in the forest and there was a beautiful fall scene and the fall scene was carried on outside. And then all of a sudden, it was after church, we heard this announcement. And we were certainly greatly disturbed about it. And within a couple of days after things kind of shook out and you were wondering what was happening and so forth, we went over and enlisted in -- enlisted in the reserve corps. And that's, with the hope, that it would enable us to finish out a year or two, not knowing, of college. We didn't know how things were going to go. As it turned out, it finished just about -- about -- I think about six months. And at Christmastime the following year, they said, Boys, don't come back after -- don't come back after your winter break because you will be called in at that time. So that -- from then on -- and by that time, all of our pals, all of our friends at home and at school had already gone, either by draft or otherwise. So we were left kind of to ourselves. And I said, you know, that gets lonesome, you know, when all your friends are gone. You are thinking, Hey, where is David and where's Jim? Well, they have already enlisted. They have taken off. They are here or there and the other place. So we were anxious to get going, and we were happy. And as Bob indicated to you probably, we enlisted in the -- or we were involved in the ROTC in the cavalry for one reason only. I love horses. That's why even today in my little art work I am known as Mr. Ed, the horse artist. And everybody who is old enough knows who Mr. Ed is. Anyway, we wanted to ride. And so this gave us the opportunity. Of course, at that time there's no thought there's going to be a war on. So we enjoyed the horse Marines there for -- on campus there for about a year -- about a year and a half. And it was all that we wanted it to be. So we were very happy with that until the war came along. And then we decided that's where we were going to be enlisted. And neither of us apparently were great -- had gone far enough to be officer material. We were still PFCs or whatever when we enlisted. So that's the way it went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I should mention to the people who are listening to this tape, the Bob you are referring to is your twin brother, Bob or Robert Storms.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And he can be heard on a different one of these oral history tapes.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Well, that's great. I will be anxious to hear his story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So you actually were in the ROTC before December 7?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Oh, yeah, right. It was strictly, do you want to be in the field artillery in the grunts, or who do you want to be with? And I said, I love to ride. Let's do it. And we thought, We have got the boots, you know. We have got the jodhpurs. Everybody will just think we are great when we go to class once a week or three times a week, whatever it was. And as we found out later on, we smelled too much of horse manure for them to get too close to us. So anyway, but we enjoyed that part of it. And that, as far as we were concerned, was our basic war experience leading in -- leading from college into going into the actual service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service, approximately?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: We were in three years. I think '42.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: I believe. I'm sorry, my --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I just -- I was trying to get a rough idea when you started your training. So might have been, what, summer of '42, or late '42, something like that?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Well, being in the cavalry, we were sent down to Fort Riley. And down there instead of -- we weren't put into the horse -- as you know, they had one horse division. But that isn't where we went. We went into the mechanized cavalry. And what we were doing at Fort Riley primarily was demolition work, and -- which I wasn't really keen about, but it didn't make any difference. We had a great time down there during -- while we were in the -- at -- at basic training down there in -- in Fort Riley. We'd go out every night or every chance we'd get to ride horses, four of us. We'd divide up in two teams. One team got five minutes head start, and then we had to go chase them. Of course, we were never allowed to come back to the same horse twice because we just brought back the animals pretty pumped up. But we had a great time. It was a lot of fun. But it was a lonesome time. And Bob was in -- was engaged at that time. And he was very sorrowful for an awful lot of times. Both of us -- twins is something a little different than normal. You have a closer kinship, I feel, with each other. And I was usually the one who was the -- either the peacemaker or the one who tried to keep everything leveled out and so forth. So -- but it was -- and he was -- and he was very -- always, every mail call, if there wasn't letters, he was upset. And if there was letters, what does she mean by this. And I said, Jeez, Bob, life is going to go on. Anyway, be that as it may, we -- our life in -- in basic training was highlighted for me. About the first day we were out to go out and dig fox holes, the -- we were out on our little maneuvers. And all of a sudden we looked up in the sky and in the far distance we saw a twister coming. It was the first time I ever seen one of those. And the first sergeant said, Dig boys, dig. And when you get in there put your rifles over your head. And if it is going to suck you out, it is going to suck you out through the trigger housing. And I was, Oh, that sounds good. Anyways, that was amazing that -- that hurricane -- not hurricane -- tornado came right down, jumped the USO, took out a bunch of barracks, jumped the chapel, and kept on going and then jumped the mess hall. And the places where most of the people to be during the daytime who weren't out actually on maneuvers was in this particular area. And that's what happened. So we thought, no, somebody up there is looking out for somebody. Anyway -- so from there, we started after our usual -- and again, here's where time bothers me. I don't -- I know I have closed out an awful lot of things, and I get very emotional about some things, especially -- I get -- I couldn't even -- I watched Private Ryan, "The Saving of Private Ryan," which I thought was the most realistic thing I have ever seen next to being shot at myself. And our granddaughter was here. And I had seen the movie and came back. And all of a sudden that night I started to cry uncontrollably. And I -- I -- and I remember when we first came home, or when I was first married and we were no children, or I guess we had just had children and we were watching some of these war stories with -- or I have forgotten who was in them, and I used to feel so comfortable. I said, I am here; I am safe; and nobody is -- nobody is going to get me or my family so I can sit here and just kind of enjoy all this shooting and pot-shotting and patrol work and all that stuff. And it was interesting how this -- I have got the complete set of "The Brothers."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: "Band of Brothers"? A Yeah. And I haven't -- I haven't seen it yet because I can't bring myself -- I don't know. I need somebody to sit with me and -- or Bob said, I've seen it. And I said, Well, then next time you and I get together, let's look at it sometime. But I have never been -- and I have had it almost two years now. And I have loaned it to other people. But it is one thing I get -- I just get turned off sometimes. My mind dates and so forth. So let's see, where are we?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you and Bob, were you in the same outfit at that point stateside?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No. We were -- during basic training we were, yeah. Because you are all lumped together. But right after we left basic training, we went out to -- I think it was out to Washington, Camp what's it, I think, in Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fort Lewis maybe?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, Fort Lewis, someplace out there, where I could look out the windows and see the mountains, Mount Hood. Anyway, he was -- and as they put you -- as you go along -- as they are calling off where -- who is going to be assigned to what troops, Bob was assigned to B troop, and I was assigned to C. And from the very first, we both tried to get -- said I want to see my troop commander and said, Can I get with B troop? And he said, Well, we'll see about that. And he went to B troop commander to see if he could get with me. And, of course, they were not going to be doing that because of the Sullivan brother deal. So as it turns out, we -- we didn't know just exactly what it was, but that's what it was. So it was kind of interesting to try. Every time we wanted to get a pass or to go home, I'd go in and tell my commander, you know, Captain, Bob is going to be free this weekend and so am I, what's the chance of getting a pass together to go with him? And he said, If his people will do it, fine. And so we went back and forth cross-roughing. So we did a lot of sight-seeing and so forth on our own. But then we started going on maneuvers. And we went down to Texas in Camp Fannin where I got a terrible infection in my ear. So I went to the hospital. And they said -- the surgeon general said, You can't go overseas. And I said, What do you mean? Because you get near any loud noise, that's going to break your ear drum for good. And he said, It is already broken part way and just taken -- it won't take much more. So I went to the captain, and I will always remember this. John Walker was the captain, the head of troop C. And he came up -- he's one of these type, Corporal Storms, are you sure you don't want to be going with your friends? You don't want to leave your friends here in the stateside now, would you, while the rest of us go out and fight for you? And inside I said, Goddamn right, I'd just as soon stay. No, I certainly can't. I'd like to be there. Somebody -- I have got a twin brother in C troop. And he said, That's right. That's right. And he said, That's who you want to be with. And I said, Okay. I said -- And so that was the -- it was one of those things. It wasn't that -- I didn't think it was that serious. But the other -- the surgeon general -- the doctor, whoever, felt that it was. But anyway, away we went. And that was our one experience. And the next thing I know we were -- we were on a train -- let's see, no, we each got -- I think we had a little furlough. I think we had a week to go home, and we took the train where -- everybody -- the trains were packed. You are sitting on your suitcases and, oh, jeez. And that was back and forth. So when we got back to camp, we decided -- or it was decided that we'd take off then for overseas. And, of course, nobody knew where. Everything looked like you are going west or to the Far East. And, of course, where we went was right up to New -- right up to New Jersey -- or, what was it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Either Camp Shanks or -- yeah, that would be New York?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: That is where we went. And we went on as security troops, which was kind of an interesting thing what you had to do. Although, I swear to goodness, I don't -- all I remember is I got seasick on the ship that we had a garbage bag on deck. Only thing I thought, I must have eaten that whole box of chocolates and that must have contributed to my downfall.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately when, I don't need exact dates, approximately when did you make the crossing -- the Atlantic crossing? This would be in '44 sometime, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yes. You know, yeah. I am trying to trace back. Because we followed in D-Day about a month after they were -- after they'd gone in. And we went on the Queen Elizabeth. Yeah, the Queen Elizabeth to -- right up to Scotland, to Glasgow, Scotland. And the one thing I remember about that was they said the townspeople had pies for us. And I thought, Oh, boy; oh, boy. And I think cherry pie or what kind of pie. Turned out to be meat pie. And that was one of the big disappointments. Anyway, but it was one of those things. And they took us right off the boat after the pie situation right on by train down to Bournemouth, England, which was right on the coast, sea coast. And that is where we went through a little training there for about two or three weeks. And then we were ready to go on the LSTs and so forth across the channel. And then we went to Cherbourg. I think that was, what, Red Beach, where we were -- in the same place where they had gone in a month and a half or so ago. And I couldn't believe -- couldn't believe how they did, how they scaled that mountain. That took, oh, my. And that was -- that was something else. That's when you first realized that the officers were the first ones in the -- when the -- when the mouth peace, when it dropped down, first ones off were the officers. And I thought, Boy, that's, you know, you always thought the officers had it cushy, but that was not true. Anyway, we went in that way. And, of course, nothing but marveling at how this -- how this ever took place, really. Hats off to them. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you spend any -- well, you said you were in England maybe just a few weeks, so you didn't get to experience much of Great Britain?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No. Oh, I think we had -- I think we had one or two passes over there. And it was -- it just wasn't that. It was cold there and just -- I don't know, an awful lot of that is just crossed off -- I remember going in once. Bob and I went in once or -- once or twice into the town there of Bournemouth. And that was the first time we experienced what fish and chips were. We didn't know. And the idea of the lights going. I mean, no -- blackouts all over at that time. It was -- it was interesting how we got home. Some of the markings in the roads would enable you to get back to your -- back to your camp. So anyway, that never -- all I remember is doing maneuvers pretty much on the beach, or calisthenics and so forth and doing different little landings and so forth. But that's -- that's all I remember there, so, until we got into France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you set up when you got into France?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: We went right into Paris. I remember my first sight of the Eiffel Tower. But I had to go to the bathroom, and there's no place to go. So there was a place out here. So just I went out and squatted down, looked up, and there was the Eiffel Tower. And I remembered that when we went back many years later to take a European trip. And I said, Nancy, this Eiffel Tower has special meaning for me. It was a cleansing point. Anyway, and from there on, then we -- as we traveled going from there on up to Luxembourg -- or, yeah, where we went right up to the -- Losheim (ph) highway right up to the national line where we took up residence, I guess, apparently just to get us used to, as it turns out now, get us used to hearing gunfire for the first time coming at you or toward you or whatever. And it was very interesting. It was -- this was the little town of Afts, A F T S. And it was just -- there were little farm communities. I mean, Grandpa lived here. His son lived here. And there's another place over here for the animals and so forth. And it was a very interesting setup. Because as we looked down and up on the hill, that's where the German pill boxes were. And they were looking down at us and we were looking up at them. And we, from then on, it was -- it was a case of patrols and so forth. A case of getting things all registered in, all -- like our -- I was in charge of mortars, well, as was Bob in his troop. And, you know, and the interesting thing about this, Bob, in doing all his pictures in this book in here, he had one in there, and I was going through them. And I said, Oops, Bob, you have an error here. What do you mean? I said, You are putting that -- that -- that mortar shell in backwards. You are putting it -- putting it nose down. I said -- I said, You don't do that. I said, If you do it, it is going to explode right down in the basement. You know, my gosh, I am glad you told me. I said, Probably nobody else except another mortar person would have known it. But I looked at his picture in here. And he had the hands were going in -- the fins and so forth were going in backwards.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, there's a picture of the two of you with the mortar. That was in Stars and Stripes?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yes, this one. That was in Stars and Stripes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was taken over there obviously, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No. No. That was taken --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stateside?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, stateside.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: It was going around maneuvers. Yeah. This --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The picture --

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Again, the picture was taken because you had twins and they took it because we both had probably very high scores in doing the thing. And, of course, he always let me know that he was three points ahead of me. Thank you, Bob. But Bob, did you ever have a chance to use your skills?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Oh, my. Anyway, let's see, we are now up in Afts. We are on the -- we are on the so-called frontline up there to get experience, to get us used to hearing live shells. Excuse me. And my -- one of the things that I was -- as I was responsible for the mortar, we had three outposts spidering out from our headquarters there, the little farm community. And so I made a log cabin for myself where I -- for my mortar, about five logs high, cut down trees and made it right in the middle of the courtyard so that I would have a -- I could predetermine -- I premarked our three outposts for the mortar and keep me from direct fire a little. So that's what I had available when we were -- when we started to -- whenever the war would start. Well, as it worked out, once we were established up there, the brass would come up at 12:00. And I would -- I would set up, and we would shoot at them. Just ran them just to get targeted in. Because there was a pill box there. You can pop one. And if anybody had to go to the can and go from one pill box to another or to the outhouse, that was -- gave us a live target to shoot at. Of course, nobody was ever hurt. We wrap up at 1:00, and they would shoot at us. So they were getting tired of that. I didn't believe it months until -- until I stayed out there once. And he popped one. He put a flare right over my head. I said, Those guys are good. Anyway. So we -- we noticed as time went on -- toward the -- right towards the -- December -- the middle of the month of December, we knew that something big was happening. And we were telegraph -- not telegraphing, we were -- we were notifying -- communicating with our rear echelon that there was a massive buildup. And they said, Oh, no. And I said, Well, our patrols show that we have got -- they are bringing bobsleds loaded with 88 millimeter shells. And there's only one thing that uses that and that is tiger tanks. And I said, We are on Losheim (ph) highway. And this has got to be the place where something is going to happen. And they said, Don't worry about it. You know, we -- we know what we are doing, or words to that effect. Anyway, we realized that -- what is happening. There wasn't any way they could take anything away from the Aachen north of us or the Roer down south, that we were just going to be left there for -- as a holding for us. And whether they thought it was a bigger -- a bigger resistance or not would depend on what happened when the war started. And so that's what ultimately came through. But we knew that there was something big coming. And we said, Why don't they do something? Why don't they? Anyway, that's the way it was until December 16, and then that started then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that's where you were at that position?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, that's where we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was in Luxembourg?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Well, it is in that -- yeah, in the Luxembourg -- yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Am I correct? Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is it near any big cities?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not really?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No. Like Bob was in -- near Shomburg (ph), and we were near Afts. And there was Krenwinkel (ph) and a couple of other little. Now, this Bill Barton, he just loves to go over. I mean, he is an architect and he just loves to do thinking of all these things. It is a name I can give you to -- he's in Boston, and he -- oh, he would relish talking to you. But he's getting on in age, and his voice is getting lower and lower. And you have got to -- it would be interesting to get his thoughts. Another man, Grandy Davies, out of Green Bay, Wisconsin. He's the other man that went with Bill to retrace their steps. Anyway --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How far were you dug in to -- how far away were you from your brother?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: I think about two miles. He was about two miles down the line.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get to see each other much before The Bulge started?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No. No, not at all. In fact, the one thing I remember that greatly upset me was during -- just before -- just before The Bulge started, he made me a Christmas card with a little GI with a little -- bent over a Christmas tree and so forth. And it had all the names and so forth on it. And when The Bulge started they said, Burn everything. And I said, I can't burn that. They said, Burn everything. So that's what happened. I will remember that. That -- that was -- is something that I hated. It was the last contact I was going to have with him until -- until I -- until after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know he was captured at that point?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: I didn't -- when the war started -- well, I will put this in now at this point. At the end of the first day of the Battle of the Bulge, I heard from B troop, or I tried to find out. And I talked with a couple of the guys. I said, What about Bob? How is he doing? And he said, the last they heard from Bob he was in the ditch and firing up a storm. And then -- and then my transmission went out and that was all we heard. So I had no idea. But what I did, I wrote to my folks and to Bob's fiance at that time, Janet. I must have written two or three times a week to each of them. Not that the letters necessarily got out, but when they did, they went out in the pail telling them that you will hear from Bob in -- by Easter. I knew it was three months. And I said, Takes that long for the grave diggers to get around and tag everybody. So I said, If he is dead, mom and dad have that much time to hope. And if they don't -- I mean, if he's not -- if he is not dead, then the hope is great. But as it turned out, on Good Friday, I think it was April 20, whatever it was when he was -- he found out -- they -- my mom and dad heard that he was alive, that he was a prisoner of war. And I thought, Well, that's the greatest thing. I don't want to call another one. That's great. But I didn't know that until the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think Bob told me the story that you were looking for him in the piles of men, in the casualties, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were looking for him because you thought he was dead?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. I mean, every place we'd go, I wasn't sure. I wasn't sure if -- all I know, they wanted to send me home. And I said, No, I want to stay here. I want to say here, remain here and look for my brother, I said, along with everything else what we are doing. So that worked out. And so -- but every place we went and every chance I got, we had to get to any -- where there were any radio people or connections then, How is B troop, and so forth? Haven't heard anything. And, of course, hadn't heard anything. I knew a lot of the guys in his outfit because -- and he knew a lot of them in ours, because we'd go back and forth. So it wasn't if they were wondering Bob who or Ed who. They knew that I knew a lot of his guys. In fact, at the reunion now, I am always included in B troop's group right along with C troop.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not to get too graphic, but I think Bob told me that you were looking at the bodies of dead GIs because you thought possibly --

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, that must have been tough.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Oh, that is. And then when you see -- and then when you see, especially during -- after Malmedy and you see how they are cutting ring fingers off, oh, my. That's when I think the Americans really got pissed off enough to say, This is a real war. You know, this is desecration of human bodies. And everybody got -- I will never forget after the war was going on, I mean, after The Bulge was going on and we had been -- it had been a couple of weeks, and I ran into a sergeant from the 82nd who was sitting down there and just kind of taking a breather. And I said, Sarge, how far are they going? He stood up and said, This is where they stop. And, you know, the hair went up in the back of my head. And I said, My God, I think he means it. And that's when you realized that everybody was upset. They were really, I mean, there was no longer fear. It was just mad, you know, what's happening on this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What happened to you next during the Battle of the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Oh, the next -- oh, well, let's see here, we were -- as we were first -- the first thing of the Battle of the Bulge started we were told, You will stay and fight until the last man. And I said, Holy mackerel. I said, This is a movie. I said, This isn't Ed Storms. Next thing I saw Lieutenant Miller came riding in on his armored car. And bingo, he got, ugh. And he was dead. And he was the first one shot in our organization. And I am like, Oh, boy. And we stayed there until -- for about eight hours. And finally got the word it is time for a strategic withdrawal. And they were already coming through the barns on one side, and we were on the other. And my jeep had been blown out. So there's no place for me to get but jump on the back of an armored car. And this one armored car couldn't -- I was on top, and there was no protection around, you know, but it was a free ride, but they couldn't get it going. So puff, puff. I said, Get this rascal going. Jeez, I said, There's nothing saving me up here. So finally chug, chug, chug, chug, went down a hill and got going. And we -- just as they came bursting through that part of it. We got through there. And we went for about another mile through a wooded area. And I said -- we went through it expecting this is the place where they should nail our hides but good, and they didn't. We don't understand why they didn't get on either side and just pick us off like road kill. You know, why not? But they didn't. And we got through. They must have thought we were all through. Well, the thing that upset us again initially was the 106th TDs decided they were going to move out. And they said, We are not going to let these valuable guns be captured. So they said, We are taking off. So they pulled out on both flanks. So left us there. So here we are. We had this over here. And boy, I said, Where do you guys think you are going? They said, We are not going to get these things captured. I said, What about us? And they said, Tough. And, well, you know, you say many things in times like that. Anyway, you hate to see your flanks being totally cut off. Anyway, we -- we moved about two miles over in some other -- down the road past the wooded areas and so forth. And they finally said, Ed, take a few people and go up along this fence line and report back what's happening. Well, I looked out there and I said I can tell you what's happening from here. I don't have to -- of course, you don't say that. You go out there. And the next thing I see is these tiger tanks coming over the hills like this, those big snouts just running up and down. And I said, Oh, my. And at first, they started using -- they saw us. And so, you know, Hey, this is target practice for them. They shoot one and they make a big hole. And the one thing I yelled out, I said, the only thing I learned from basic training, if they shoot at you with a gun like that, go get in the hole because chances are they never hit the same place twice. And I said, I hope this is a truism. So after that first shot, I went and jumped in that hole. We stayed there until about -- until we were ordered back on the -- by radio to come back. And that night we got into this little town there, little barren -- little brick barracks or something. I don't even know the name of the town. It wasn't Poteau (sp). But the first sergeant wanted volunteers. And for the first time, I felt sorry for him. Ernie Oswald was the acting first sergeant. The other guy had a problem. I don't know where he was. And I said, We need somebody who's checked out on the 50-caliber, and we are going out to look for paratroopers. And I finally said, Okay. And I thought, What am I doing here, you know. And I thought, you know, if you hadn't -- if you haven't had the experience, if -- what you don't know can't hurt you, you know. So you go out. And fortunately, I say fortunately, we didn't run into anything. But we got back that night. And I heard a couple of the other guys saying, you know, Hey, that wasn't Storms' job, that was ours. We are checked out on that. They said he has got mortars. When it is mortar time, he does the work. So anyway, so that we -- that was something we went through. And the next thing we were ordered back up. We had lost most of our -- a lot of our vehicles, and our food, and our ammunition. We were told, Get in line; go back up, we just need somebody; we just need to plug somebody into the area. And this was at Poteau. We were lined up going out of town on that one. That's where I figured our lieutenant was very brave. He was an English professor -- English teacher in high school, I think it was high school or college. I am not sure. But a very precise person, very nice, nice guy, not the type of guy you expect that you really want. You want a tough guy. You don't want any guy you'd bring home, but you want somebody that you want on your side out there. Well, Max Crawford was a gem, a jewel, a lovely guy, a very nice man. And he said -- came back by me. I was sitting in my jeep waiting for something to happen. And he said, Storms, get a bazooka. I said, I don't have one. He said, Here's one. I will thank you. We are going up here. There's something up here. I don't know what it is. It is at the head of our column. I am going up and I am going to yell "halt." If it doesn't halt, let go of this thing and then we will see what happens. So we crept up and he got out his little English "halt." And gosh with that, it was a tiger tank. We ran smack in -- we were nose to nose. I fired the bazooka. And from then on, all hell broke loose. We were nose to nose. This is in Poteau. We were half mile outside of the little town. The town was about four buildings, you know, when you say towns. And everybody, as soon as it started to shoot, everybody got out of their jeeps and fled to the sides, over to the wood line. Well, of course, the guys who are our guys in the ring mounts and armored cars thought they were Germans. So we started shooting our own people. Until we yelled, Hold it, these are our guys. So we started coming back. So this went on who knows how long. And we finally got back and started going to the rear back to the town, set up some kind of a return fire program for them. And we got halfway up there, and I ran into this guy, Fisher -- no, yeah, Al Fish. And he was wounded. And he said, I can't make it across. And I said, Get on my back. I mean, I can haul you. He's too big to carry, but I could haul him. I said, we can either go straight across the short way right across the square, or we can go all of the way around and take our chances that way. And he said, Let's go straight across. And I said, Okay. He's on my back. I kept thinking, God, you are going to protect me. I have got somebody on my back. I am doing a good thing. You know, but, you know, you do think about what are your chances, but we made the shot there, so, whistlings and so forth. But we got across and got him into this building where he could be cared for by our medics. Interesting things happen. You came back out and there was an armored car right there out in front of the building after I left Fish out. And he -- I thought -- it was looking down the road and I could see the Germans on one side crossing over to go into the little church and come up this way. And so I got down and was shooting. As they crossed the road, I would shoot at them, you know. All of a sudden somebody came shooting right over my head. And I said, Uh, oh, somebody knows where I am. So I got down a little lower and was shooting out between the front underneath the armored car. And the next thing I know, they shot back. After I shot, they shot. I think I said I think he knows where I am. There's got to be a better vantage point. So we got up in the building and started to shoot from up in there. I went inside. And one of our -- one of our men had been hit by a bazooka and his leg was hanging just by a piece of meat about as big as my thumb, the knee here, and the rest of the leg down here. And I was carrying him and holding both sides as we are laying him down. I had my gun on my shoulder in a sling. And I just -- as we got him down, it came down and hit him right on the leg. And I felt, Oh, God, you gonna -- it hurt me more than it did him. He said, Don't worry about it, Ed. That bazooka seared off those nerve endings. I have got no feeling there. I said, Thank you for that. I said, Do you want me to take this apart? He said, No, my father is a surgeon. He is out here someplace. Chances are he can save the leg. Well, I don't know if he ran into his father, whoever it was, though, they did save his leg. Because he came back after the war while we were still in Germany before we left for home. And he came back. He was ready to -- he was going to be -- he was no longer able to serve -- to serve in any capacity, but he was able to walk. So that's what we had there. Well, the final thing on Poteau was we were there all day, and from early morning. And it was time for us -- everybody was saying it is time to leave. We are ready to go. So this good friend of mine, my buddy, Bob Bunts from Farmington, New York, he and I were together. And we jumped in this jeep. It was the last one out of there. It was loaded with the guys. You know how everybody is, Hey, don't forget me, and jump on and take off. Well, it hit the ditch, and Bunts and I rolled. We were the top two that rolled off. So we went back in because they were coming up in the road. So we went back in the barn. And we were padding the horse because they were shooting through the other end of the barn. I said, Bunts, are we just going to stay here or are we going to get out? I said, That armored car out there, do you think we can make that thing work? I don't know, he says, Let's try. He tried it and it worked. And chug, chug, chug, chug, got around the corner. Here comes the guys with their Panzerfausts, and looked down the road. Gosh, they looked at us and said, Jeez, there's still somebody alive in there. So they started ringing a lot of small arms fire, but I saw those Panzerfausts, those babies, we are going to be -- we are going to be cooked geese in here. I said, Bob we can run faster. So we jumped out of the hatch and started running down the road. We had the protection of the vehicle a little bit. So we had a little head start. And we heard them laughing up there. And we are like, My gosh, we ran down the road while the krauts said, Let go, we will get them later on. And as we got down the road a couple of miles, we saw some of our own people coming up the road. They were not our people, but recruits coming in to take our place. Of course, they all had that worried look, How was it? Ah, piece of cake. If you told them what it was, they'd turn around and go back. I said that's the direction we aren't going. So that's where that took care of Poteau. And from there on, things were -- after that little bit, we saw -- that's -- a day or two after that is when I ran into that 82nd guy, the sergeant who said they are going to stop right here. And we -- I lost track of our guys and -- Bunts and I both did -- of our outfit. Because they had taken off while we were still back in the barn waiting our chance to get out. And so I hooked up with a tank group. I asked them if they -- how about my sticking with you until we find our group. And they said, Yeah, happy to have you, you know. It came nightfall. You can sleep in the tank. And I said, I don't sleep in tanks. I am a cavalry man. There's a house. He said, Where you going? I said, The house up there. That's where I am going. So Bunts and I went up there. Anyway, and from there on it is hazy. I remember going through towns and running through people. Of course, you are constantly looking -- we all look alike. You know, it is not as if somebody had a red hat or somebody had a green hat or something and looking for each other. Of course, they had taken off all of the identification of the vehicles so you couldn't see 14th cavalry or 18th recon or anything. So it was some time before we finally found our -- oh, yeah, we heard about, we were one of the last ones to get by the Germans who were directing people into Bastogne. And we didn't -- many of our people were -- did have a side trip to Bastogne, which was a tremendous achievement for those guys to hang in there. So, I am out of gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the Battle of the Bulge wound down after that, I assume?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After the air strikes and that sort of thing, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. And -- oh, and that was the thing. There was no -- no air support. Although I was interested to hear in Bob's story in here that they had air support for one strafing. And we saw none of it. First we saw -- I forgot the days when it was. But it was -- it was wonderful when they came over -- the sky was dark with them, with those B-17s. And, oh, that was, Everybody, Go, go, you know. It was really something else. And that's where I finally got my good warm jacket. We had a plane was shot down and we were over there. And one of the guys could no longer in need of his flight jacket so that's what I had. Now, let's see --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, yeah, after the Bulge then?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah. That stopped -- I think that pretty much stopped the Bulge. We went back to Liege, Belgium where we were re-outfitted and got ready to go back in again and start. It was interesting how in going through the -- anything in France, the French left all of the tile, all of the crap and the corruption, the bombed-out debris right where it was waiting for us to come by. You go through the Germans, you bomb them, even though they are the enemy, the home folks, they are out there putting the tile back on their roofs and getting everything set up. I mean, they -- you had to admire them for an awful lot of things. You began to worry about the kids as you would get closer to Germany. Or when we got into Germany, we had to be very careful. Because the kids, these pig stickers, this long, they were -- we just heard about them, and then we finally ran into them when we got into Germany after we crossed the Rhine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were they exactly?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Long knives, yeah. The youth there, I forgot what they call them. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, then basically wasn't it almost like a suicide attack, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Well, yeah, oh, yeah, little kid. Well, I don't know how suicide. Well, it turned out to be there. It would be there. But they usually would take somebody with them. Because they are young people, you want to give them candy or give them some --
[END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE BEGINNING OF SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE]

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, let's see. Yeah, let me think. This is where I -- I get -- gets not -- gets hazy, just a lot of it drops. I haven't thought of it in years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just say anything that comes to mind. If you can't remember the exact sequence, that's fine.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, I can't. I remember one time we went into this little town. It was right on -- let's see here, we hadn't crossed the Rhine yet. It was before -- I am trying to think of the river. And it was down the river and up the other side. This little village, we stopped right in the street or in the little cobblestone roads in our jeeps and stuff. And we got out of -- Max Crawford said, I think we better get out of here. We look like we are in the line of fire. Somebody may be shooting at us from down across the river. Well, the way it worked out, we just got out and pop, pop, pop, right -- boy, that was a providential save there as we got ourselves all of the way up the -- got out of the vehicle. And they said, Boy, they said, that's where -- that's what needs to be cleaned out. So we were ready to go. Along comes some infantry, some little squirts, you know, all shapes and sizes. And I tell you, another thrilling moment, they said -- they said, Where are they? I said, Down there. And they said, Let's go get 'em. And they went. And I said, Now, that is true courage. You know, really, I mean, there they are, Let's get 'em. That's what needs to be done. And I never -- from that time on, never failed to -- if I saw an infantryman, want a ride, take a ride. I have got a ride for you. Because those people had great courage. Great courage. But we eventually passed through different areas. And we got down near Remagen. And we were -- they -- they were -- they -- they -- they had just scaled -- they had made it across and the most beautiful sight in all of the world was the flag on the other side. Just, it was -- it was just patriotically humbling to see it. We were the first ones across on the pontoon, pontoon bridge that they made. We were there while they were making it. As soon as they made it, we got over. Once you got on the other side of the Rhine, they were done. It was one of those things that was, you know, we knew we were -- we were in command and they were on the run. And we just -- you began to start worrying about walking on eggs, you know. I don't know how much longer it is going to last, but whatever. We wanted to be around here. Don't want to take a stray. So let's see --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you found out about your brother actually being -- all that time he was listed as missing in action, right?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You found out about him in April, you say?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: No, I didn't find out until May 7.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, you didn't; your family found out?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Yeah, mom and dad did. Well, of course, that was April 27. And this was May 7. So we are talking three -- we are talking about a week or something, yeah. So they hadn't had a chance to hear anything. Oh, was that a joy. And it is interesting where we wound up. We wound up in Salzburg, Austria. And we started -- we were leading -- we were leading the point for one final assault on Salzburg. We knew it was getting close, but we didn't know exactly what -- and the infantry was behind us, and we were running the point. And I saw a tank across the valley hidden in the trees. And I thought, Oh, let's go take a look. I got down behind a tree and was looking at it. Next thing I know he come right over my head. And it was my driver, Ted McDonald. He had shot -- he had used his 88 -- his gram rifle to shoot at the tank. And I thought the guy was shooting back at me. I said, Goddamn it, that's the last unlimbered musket. Good grief. Anyway, we went out a little further. As we got into a hill going into town, here came all the towns people, all hands up, thousands of them. And we looked -- we looked behind to see where the Army was. They had already fallen off. They were no longer behind us. So we were by ourselves and the whole thing. The officers took charge of all people. Just turned around and go back and take it easy and, you know. So that's the way the war ended. And it was such a wonderful feeling that night. We were camped back up in the woods, but to go walk out on those lonely roads and still find something, find peace and quiet and not worry about being sniped. Now, that's the thing that bothers me about the current war over in Iraq. The war is over, but it is more dangerous now than ever before. So, anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So any big celebrations that night? Or was everybody just relieved?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Everybody was just relieved, yeah. Yeah. And, of course, we were way out in the boonies. They celebrated after we got into town. Yeah, we were supposed to -- after the war was over, we were supposed to be show troops. You know, if they were going to have a parade or something, we'd be in all that. Well, they screwed up so badly. Good grief. They had -- they had a gang rape, bad scene. And they got everybody lined up in a row in front of the buildings. And the girls were coming down picking out the ones. If you don't think that isn't a time to be concerned. You know, after all, the girl can say, You, you, and you. And what recourse do you have? They didn't have DNA then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So I assume they picked somebody?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Oh, they did, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he get a fair trial? Or how did they prove it?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Well, I think they released him to the local people, yeah. And then they got -- for us, they decided we were going to go back to get a 30-day rehab and go to Japan. But -- but what was it, 46 -- 85th, I think, was going over there. Anyway, we were in Muskogee, Oklahoma. We came home and had our 30-day rehab. And my folks couldn't understand why I was so nervous, pacing up and down in front of the house, you know. And it was August 14 and that was the day I was supposed to be back, and that was the day the war ended. And that was the day they said, Don't bother coming back for a couple of days. Oh, my. But the ship left without us. So we went -- the guys who were already down in camp went. Thank heavens for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you were still --

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: We were still here. And we got out. We went to -- sent us to Camp Ataberry (ph) where we awaited discharge. While I was there for a week, they put me in the MPs, you know, to do something rather than sit in the barracks. Those -- and, of course, they didn't like -- if you had any service -- overseas stripes, any overseas action at all, they didn't care for that. You know, they weren't -- so when we get a call for -- they had a couple of calls for disturbance, a man beating up on a girl in the hotel next door. I said, Well, let's go. And he said, No, let's -- we will smoke a cigarette. When the cigarette is done, then we go. Then chances are it is all over. So that's the way our -- and then they put me as MP in a burlesque house to take care of the balcony. I said, Oh, jeez, this is, I mean, this is no place for a war-torn veteran to go. Anyway --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally see your brother then?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: I didn't see him until the day I got home -- oh, let me think just a minute. Let me think here. Oh, Bob beat me home by about a week. And because he -- it would have been three weeks, because he was supposed to have been flown home. But he got yellow jaundice. So I saw him the night I got home, which was probably three weeks after he did. And dad was home and drove me, and we drove up to Battle Creek, which is about two hours away. And that was the first I'd seen him, so -- his favorite song then was "Don't fence me in." So I -- I really don't have an awful lot. I know one thing our group -- our 14th Cavalry has been very upset that we never got a -- that we didn't get a presidential citation along with everybody else. And we said, Our blood was just as red and flowed just as fast as everybody else's. And I said, It wasn't our fault that we were put in an area that was indefensible. I mean, we stayed there until we were told to come back, you know. So everybody -- so what we did a couple of times ago, we had -- we decided to have -- if we weren't going to have a presidential citation, we would make one of our own. So this is -- this is the little badge that we -- that one of the guys picked out, Seamore Caplan, and this is the citation that we have. And we thought that that would be something that would --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great. Did Bob do the illustration?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Bob did the illustration, and I did the writing and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: That's always been the way we worked. I have always been the writer, and he has been the artist.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: It has been. Of course, I love to -- I love to -- to draw also. And, of course, the only thing I draw is horses. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about World War II, any other vivid memories come to mind, random memories that you haven't shared yet?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: Gosh, I can't -- I can't think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We have covered it?

sp.speaker: Edmund B. Storms
sp.p: I think so. [END SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE]
